lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Jul 2022
- Ran the checkout A/B test until significance by checking the p-value every day and stopping on the first day it fell below 0.05.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; my findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Writes the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
- Cut the monthly revenue report from 3 days of spreadsheet work to 2 hours by moving it to scheduled SQL queries and a shared dashboard.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.

- Joining 40 source tables, deduplicating customer records across two loyalty systems and rebuilding the attribution logic in dbt-style SQL models, raised the share of orders tied to a campaign from 58% to 81%.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Trained 20 merchandisers to answer their own questions with the self-serve dashboards, halving ad hoc data requests.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Modeled hourly bike-share demand for 120 stations from 2 years of public trip data, forecasting next-day demand within 12% mean absolute error.
- Cut empty-station hours from 300 to 200 a week, a 50% reduction, in a replay of last summer's rebalancing.
- Raised forecast hit rate by 15% across 120 stations, from 60% to 75%, by adding weather and event features.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table and matched repeat visitors, giving the pantry its first count of unique households.
- Wrote a one-page guide the pantry coordinator used to update the visit table each month after the project ended.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: Date of birth and nationality should be removed.
items.because: They are personal details a reader is not meant to weigh and can distract from the candidate’s qualifications.

items.says: Experience should appear before Education.
items.because: The current ordering puts Education before established analyst work.

items.says: Experience entries should be in newest-first order.
items.because: The older Pinecrest role appears above the more recent Brightcart role, making the chronology harder to scan.

items.says: The test’s stopping rule is statistically invalid as written.
items.because: Stopping when a repeatedly checked p-value first falls below 0.05 inflates the overall Type I error rate.

items.says: The bullet gives the test process but not its outcome or resulting change.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what the experiment established or whether it improved checkout performance.

items.says: The bullet does not say what analysis identified the evening peak.
items.because: The reader can see the data source but not how the analysis supported the staffing decision.

items.says: The first-person pronoun makes the staffing result indirect.
items.because: “My findings” obscures the action and conflicts with the résumé’s phrase-style bullets.

items.says: This bullet should lead the Pinecrest entry.
items.because: The staffing change and reduction in hold time are the entry’s strongest result.

items.says: “Writes” is present tense even though the role ended in July 2022.
The unrelated duty list delays the time-saving result.
items.because: A scanning reader must pass ancillary duties before reaching the main contribution and its measurable value.

items.says: The dashboard bullet does not describe the analytical or technical work used to build it.
items.because: A reader can see the deliverable but not the data or analysis that demonstrates the candidate’s skills.

items.says: A null customer name does not identify customers with no orders.
items.because: A left join preserves the customer name when no order matches; the check should use a non-nullable order-side field.

items.says: The bullet foregrounds the join method without saying what the finding led to.
items.because: A reader cannot tell why identifying these customers mattered to the business.

items.says: The long gerund phrase obscures who did the work and delays the result.
items.because: It makes the work the grammatical subject and weakens the impact of the increase from 58% to 81%.

items.says: “dbt-style SQL models” may not be clear outside the team.
Reporting MAE as 12% without a denominator or normalization is not interpretable.
items.because: MAE is measured in demand units, and a percentage needs a defined reference value.

items.says: The bullet does not say what modeling approach produced the forecast.
items.because: A reader cannot see the main analytical skill behind the result or what kind of model was built.

items.says: The change from 300 to 200 hours is about a 33.3% reduction, not 50%.
items.because: The decrease of 100 hours is about one-third of the 300-hour baseline.

items.says: The bullet does not say what rebalancing change was tested.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what decision or change led to the result.

items.says: The bullet does not make clear that the reduction was simulated.
items.because: The result could be read as observed rather than produced by a replay.

items.says: The increase from 60% to 75% is 15 percentage points, not 15%.
items.because: Relative to the starting rate of 60%, the increase is 25%.

items.says: The bullet does not define what counts as a forecast “hit.”
items.because: Readers cannot tell what counted as a correct forecast, making the hit rate hard to interpret.

items.says: The bullet does not state the number of unique households identified.
items.because: The 9,000 logs show the input’s scale, not the deduplicated result or its usefulness.
